chapter_theme: General songs (பொதுப்பாடல்கள், 13 of 21), sung at no named shrine: most confess the poet's bondage to courtesans who rob, drug and discard a man, and ask Murugan to end the infatuation; others ask for the reality beyond sects and scriptures, for the feet before Death or the scribe's fate comes, and for knowledge that roots out the bonds; the praise turns on Krishna, Rama and Siva, Murugan's own love-sickness for Valli, and Murugan as teacher of Siva.
structure_note: Courtesan songs: 1172, 1173, 1176, 1178, 1180, 1181, 1182, 1183, 1185; 1176 and 1183 share a 'showing' (காட்டி, காட்டுவர்) refrain. 1174 asks whether the ascetic's fall is fate or grace. 1175 and 1177 ask for the reality the sects cannot reach; 1179 is a litany of சாமி; 1184 is the householder's cares before Death; 1186 asks for knowledge that roots out the malas.

1172.reading: The poet describes dancing women with pearl strings on their breasts, harsh eyes and a great appetite for wealth, who give their lips' nectar to young men struck by Kama's sugarcane bow, and asks whether his wandering, caught in their cheating and lost to grace, will not end so that he may cling to Murugan's feet. The praise names the war on the mad elephant-faced demon where ghouls play in blood and the eighteen hosts dance, Murugan's love for the kuravar girl born to a sage absorbed in tapas, and the guru who named a stubborn poet 'egg' and won a poem from him.
1172.nuance: மெத்தத் திரவிய பட்சத்தியர், women very fond of money, makes them the paid women. முற்பட்ட முரட்டுப் புலவனை முட்டைப் பெயர் செப்பிக் கவிபெறு refers to a story of Murugan mocking a proud poet that I cannot identify with confidence; the deer (உழை) and the sage point to Valli's birth.

1173.reading: The poet describes women who dance and sing, rob many men and then pick quarrels to drive them out, weep and rub their eyes as if in love, and are Death in the shape of desire with glances like arrows; perfumed with lilies, musk and rosewater in the south wind, he falls on their breasts and melts till dawn, and asks whether a day will come when Murugan protects him. The praise names Siva with Parvati at his side, Krishna bound to the mortar by the cowherd women for stealing butter, Indra on his elephant who came to worship, and Murugan who was angry with Brahma, guarded the gods' city, toppled Krauncha and routed the demons.
1173.nuance: பலர் பொருள் கவர்ந்து இடை கலாமிட்டு ஓட்டிகள, they take many men's wealth and drive them out with a quarrel, is the Naladiyar's picture of the courtesan. ஆசைக் கூற்றிகள் and பார்வைக் கூற்றினர் call the women Death. விபுதர்பதி அங்கதலம் மேவிச் சாற்றிய தமிழ்நூல் seems to tie the south wind to a hill where Tamil was first told, perhaps Pothigai; that is uncertain.

1174.reading: The poet says that though he studied without fault, renounced to end hostile karma and sat in many yogas, Kama's fragrant arrows wore him down until he was ready to ride the palmyra horse, and he melted for women weeping with acting eyes; he asks whether this ruin is the fate of his former deeds or the will of Murugan's grace, for in his confusion he cannot tell. The praise names the father present in the Veda and in all things, Vishnu who came from the pillar in two forms and split Hiranya's chest, Murugan as his nephew and as son of Siva, and the lord who ran into the millet field for the forest deer-girl.
1174.nuance: The song's question is explicit: முற்பயந்த விதிவசமோ, மற்றை உன்றன் அருள்வசமோ, fate of past deeds or your grace's will? It is left unanswered. That the renouncer and yogi is the one who agrees to ride the madal (பனைமடல் ஊர்தற்கு இசைந்து) turns the akam lover's last resort into an ascetic's fall. ஞானக் குருந்து may recall the kuruntham tree of 7.

1175.reading: The poet describes a reality that cannot be held, cannot be glimpsed by practitioners or spoken by debaters, is not caught in the five elements, is not reached by other means, by imagined meditation, by the ladder of the desiring mind or by the path of books, nor stated by reasons, a great ocean of bliss, and asks whether he will bow to Murugan's sandal-scented feet. The praise names the vel driven into golden Meru to end Indra's danger, the rule of the world's circle under the shade of a single umbrella, Murugan who wears on his head the jewelled anklet feet of the hunter girl, and the teacher who first made Siva read the word that cannot be read.
1175.nuance: The plea is built from negatives (படாது, ஒணாது, தகாது, பெறாது), a way of naming the One by what cannot reach it. வாசிக்கப் படாத வாசகம், the unread word, taught to Siva is the Om story, though Om is not named. கிராதை நூபுர ... பாதசேகர, he who wears Valli's feet as a crown, reverses the usual devotee's posture.

1176.reading: The poet lists what women show a man, reading milky speech, loosening their clothes, seating him on the bed, giving their lips, opening the books of love, rolling their eyes, pressing their nails and showing their tricks, and asks that Murugan end his delusion for them and show him the greatness of thinking of his feet. The praise uses the same refrain of showing for Siva, who kicked Death, danced in the forest at the end of time, held the poison and burned Kama, and for Murugan, who in the hunters' millet field showed himself worn with love, embraced the deer-girl and showed the skill of a happy life.
1176.nuance: The verb காட்டி ends almost every phrase on both sides of the song: the women display their arts, Siva displays his deeds, and the poet asks Murugan to display (காட்டி) the eminence of the feet. தோதகம் is deceit. Some phrases of the Valli part (வாலிபம் இளைத்து) are hard to construe.

1177.reading: Calling on the lord of the cock banner who fought the Nirutar and Krauncha and wed the kuravar girl, the poet asks that with tears pouring from both eyes and a mind brimming with love, as the body of elements, the life within it and the inner faculties fall away and he himself is lost, he may know by awareness what the debaters and sects call 'it is' and 'it is not'. The praise names Kama with his makara banner, Tamil breeze from the Malaya hills, flower arrows and sugarcane bow, burned by the eye of Siva, and Murugan as the son given by Abhirami, Sankari, the mountain daughter, delight of the gods' elephant-girl.
1177.nuance: யானும் இழந்த இடந்தனில் உணர்வாலே, by awareness in the place where I too am lost, puts knowledge after the loss of body, breath, faculties and self, not after argument. ஆமென அன்றென நின்றதை, that which stands as both 'yes' and 'no', is what the sects dispute.

1178.reading: The poet describes women who knit their brows, flash carp eyes, spread their hair, wave bangled hands, lead a man to an aloe-scented bed in a crystal chamber, embrace him, mark him with nails and give the nectar of their lips, and asks whether, rid of the madness these melting women give, he will strive to worship Murugan. The praise is a long portrait of Siva, the dancer, burner of Tripura, holder of the poison, Ganga on his head, Uma's lord on the mountain, who cuts birth, smears cremation ash, rides the bull and burned Madana, and names Murugan as born of his boundless grace.
1178.nuance: உருக்கிகள், the women who melt a man, and தருபித்து, the madness they give, frame the plea, which is only to try (முயல்வேனோ) to worship. Murugan is called the one who arose within Siva's compassion (க்ருபைக்குள் உதித்தருள்).

1179.reading: The poet confesses that he does not know the sight that those who think of Murugan's feet attain, falls in with the deceiving sectarians who twist the path, has no skill to sing his praise and whirls in sin like a lazy dog, and asks whether Murugan does not know the account of service due to him in this troubled world. The praise is a litany of சாமி: the lord of Sivam, who dances on the peacock, shines within us, ends birth, forgives faults, grinds the demons to dust, ordains our service, and the one of Saravana who is called 'the father's Swami'.
1179.nuance: தகப்பன் சாமி, his father's lord, is the title from the story of Murugan teaching Siva. எனக்கு உண்டாகு பணிவிடை கணக்கு, the reckoning of service that falls to me, asks to be given work rather than release. The first lines (காலதரிசனை, புலக்கண், புழுக்கண் பாவம்) are hard to construe.

1180.reading: The poet says he gives no thought to what would end the pleasure he takes in women's carp eyes, fragrant hair and pot-like breasts, but quarrels with all, spends his days and whirls like a spun top until he falls; he asks Murugan to end his fear of the hour life leaves. The praise names the destruction of the Sura clans so that Indra and the gods were freed, the sea trembling and Meru crumbling, and Murugan who, pained by the south wind, evening and Kama's attack, went to the hunters' millet field and bowed to the dark-eyed Valli.
1180.nuance: The same south wind and Kama that drive the poet to women make Murugan himself love-sick (வேடை எனும்படி சிந்தை நொந்திட) for Valli: the song puts the god in the lover's place. The top (பம்பரம்) spinning and falling is the poet's life.

1181.reading: The poet says he cannot cross the ocean of desire for proud pleasure-women with carp eyes and ear-studs, or the ocean of tantra, ritual, Veda and Agama whose shore he never sees; he has not sung the anklet feet and has no love, yet asks the guru for grace. The praise names the saving of Indra's city, the end of the night-walkers, the mountain split and the sea roaring as the vel broke the mango, and Murugan in the millet field begging the hunter's girl to save his life from the south wind and Kama's flower arrows.
1181.nuance: The two oceans are set side by side: desire (ஆசை என்கிற பாராவாரம்) and the endless scriptures (தந்த்ர க்ரியா வேதாகம கலையாய ஆழி); neither can be crossed, and the poet admits even love is lacking (நேசிலன்). Murugan's own plea to Valli, காமவிடாய் கெடும்படி காவாய் ஆவியை, echoes the poet's.

1182.reading: The poet speaks of dancing women who cast nets of eyes that look like Death and poison and melt only at the sight of gold, and of his enslavement in their embrace, and asks whether, his infatuation ended, there will be a day when he praises the sacred hills, among them Sonagiri, Kathirai and the Kundram. The praise names the hunters with their bows who bow at the lotus feet, and the deer-girl who scared the birds from the millet field, with whom Murugan spends his days with ever-new companions.
1182.nuance: பொன்கண்டு இளகு கூத்திகள், dancing girls who soften at the sight of gold, makes them the paid women. The list of hills in lines 576 to 579 is too garbled to read with confidence; சோண (Sonagiri, Tiruvannamalai) and கதிரை (Kathirkamam) are the clearest names.

1183.reading: The poet lists what common women show young men, rolled eyes, swaying breast-chains, loosened hair, smiles, slipping clothes, dancing feet, and how they embrace them till they melt, strip them of all they own, give drugs that burn the belly and draw out their very life; he asks whether Murugan will not free him from that union and take him. The praise names Krishna who kicked the marutha trees, broke the cowherd women's pots, was beaten with a rope and wept, split Hiranya's chest and held up the hill against the rain, and Murugan his nephew whose vel tore Sura's kin and whose lotus feet are praised.
1183.nuance: பொதுமாதர், women common to all, and உடைமை அடையவே பறித்து, stripping a man of everything he owns, are explicit; பொடிமாயம் and மருத்திட்டு ஆட்டிகள் add the love-drug, as in 1161. காட்டுவர் closes every phrase of the first half, as காட்டி does in 1176.

1184.reading: The poet speaks of the children he must support and the wife who must be fed, the toil of seeking gold and the mind's great agitation, all as the chain Brahma writes decrees, and asks that before Death comes to the burning ground to take his life, he may praise 'Kanda of the sandal shoulders' and Murugan end his torment and give his feet. The praise names Siva the skull-bearer who took blows from Arjuna, rode the bull, burned Kama with his eye, danced in the fire and swallowed the poison, and Murugan who gave him the meaning, and who gives his loving devotees release from sin and a fearless heart.
1184.nuance: வண்போதன் தீட்டும் தொடரது படியே, according to the chain the lotus-born writes, makes the householder's cares Brahma's script for him. பார்த்தன் கையில் அடி உண்டு is the story of Siva as the hunter struck by Arjuna. The first half is hard to construe in places (வம்பாருந் தேக்குண் டிட).

1185.reading: The poet runs through a woman's charms, the waist like Kama's bow, the elephant gait, the lotus feet, the musk-scented hair, the makara earrings, the bud-like breasts, the honey lips, the ear-long eyes, the jasmine smile and the moon forehead, and asks whether a day will come when Murugan ends the swooning infatuation he feels for every limb and takes him. The praise names Rama who bridged the sea, burned the city, ended Sita's grief and rolled the ten heads of Ravana with one arrow, Siva who burned the three cities with Meru for a bow, and Murugan who restored the gods to their city and smashed Sura and the mountain.
1185.nuance: The catalogue, each item ending in -க்கே (for the waist, for the gait ...), is itself the infatuation: அவயவம் அனைத்தூடினும் அவசமுறு மயல், a swoon at every limb. Rama and Siva are praised as Murugan's kin in one sweep.

1186.reading: The poet says that by Kama's arrows and the two kinds of deeds his body of earth and sea dances on, and asks that the maya of the mind and the hard deeds be cut away with the old impurity at its root, that he gain the joy of knowledge in experience, and play with the devotees at the feet; he asks Murugan to come before him on his steed, full of compassion and knowledge, with the gods raining flowers, bright as crores of white moons. The praise names the countless women waving fans, sun and moon as lamps, the matted sages and Vedic chanters around Siva, and Murugan his son, lord of Valli, Vishnu's nephew, the lord of Tamil.
1186.nuance: மனமாயை, இருகாழ்வினை, மலம் வேரற names the three bonds of Saiva Siddhanta (maya, karma, anava) and asks for them to be cut at the root, followed by ஞான அநுபூதி, knowledge as lived experience. The garbled யற்முதுடை (line 671) leaves one word unread.

links.note: Both make the palmyra horse the end point of love's suffering. In the Kural it is the lover's only strength; in 1174 it is what a learned renouncer and yogi is reduced to, and he asks whether fate or grace brought him there.

Both describe the truth that scriptures, practices and debaters cannot reach and call it a great ocean of bliss (மகோததி), and both answer with the feet. 1175 builds the whole plea from negatives; 1157 sets the four Saiva paths themselves among those that fail.
Both build the courtesan's arts on the verb of showing (காட்டுவர், காட்டி). 1183 adds robbery and the love-drug; 1176 turns the verb back on Siva and Murugan, asking to be shown the feet instead.

Both describe women who take all the wealth from a man's hands while he believes in their love. The Naladiyar ends in the town's laughter at the fool; 1183 ends in a plea to be taken out of that union.

Both give Murugan the love-sickness the poet confesses: the south wind and Kama's arrows wound him until he goes to Valli in the millet field. 1181 puts in his mouth the plea to save his life from love's fever.

The Naladiyar's paid women seem sweet while the man is fooled and turn harsh as a ram's horn once they are full (தாமார்ந்த போதே தகர்கோடாம்). 1173's women take the wealth of many and then pick a quarrel to drive them out (பலர் பொருள் கவர்ந்து இடை கலாமிட்டு ஓட்டிகள்), after weeping and rubbing their eyes as if in love (அன்புமுடையாரைப் போல் ... கண்பிசையும்). The song gives the same turn from feigned love to hostility and adds the false tears.

Tirumular's mirror verse says that for those who say the Lord is within and without he is within and without, and for those who say he is neither, he is neither. 1177 asks to know, by awareness in the place where body, breath, faculties and self are lost (யானும் இழந்த இடந்தனில் உணர்வாலே), what all the debaters and sects hold as 'it is' and 'it is not' (ஆமென அன்றென நின்றதை). Tirumular shows the sects finding what they assert; the song asks for that same thing by a knowing that comes only after the self is lost.

The Kural's woman says the sea of love exists and there is no raft to cross it (காமக் கடல் ... ஏமப் புணை மன்னும் இல்). 1181 cannot cross the ocean called desire (ஆசை என்கிற பாராவாரம்) and sets beside it a second ocean, of tantra, ritual, Veda and Agama, whose shore he never sees. The song keeps the Kural's sea with no crossing and adds the sea of scripture, which does not save either; only the guru's grace is left.

The Naladiyar says men without money are poison to the paid women, while a man who has worked an oil press is sugar to them if he has wealth (செய்த பொருளுடையார் அக்காரம் அன்னார்). 1182 calls them dancing girls who soften at the sight of gold (பொன்கண்டு இளகு கூத்திகள்). Both make gold the only thing that moves them; the song adds the poet's own enslavement and asks to praise the hills instead.

Tirumular says that when the body's roof falls, the women and children who ate from it do not follow; only vows and knowledge go with the dead. 1184 is the householder's life of toil for those same dependents, the children to be supported and the wife to be fed (சிறுவரும் ... துணைவியும்), and Brahma's script (வண்போதன் தீட்டும் தொடர்), and asks to praise Kanda before Death takes him at the burning ground. The song is the care Tirumular says will not follow, together with the plea to turn before it ends.

Both go through the woman part by part. 1185 lists waist, gait, feet, hair, earrings, breasts, lips, eyes, smile and forehead, each ending in -க்கே, and confesses a swoon at every limb (அவயவம் அனைத்தூடினும் அவசமுறு மயல்). The Naladiyar lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinew and skin and asks which of these is the garlanded woman (எத்திறத்தாள்). The same catalogue serves the infatuation in the song and its cure in the Naladiyar.

Tirumular names the three impurities, anava, maya and karma, as bran and husk around the sprouting grain, and tells the soul to separate its bonds. 1186 asks for the same three to go: the mind's maya (மனமாயை), the two hard deeds (இருகாழ்வினை) and the old impurity cut at the root (மலம் வேரற). The song names what follows the cutting, the joy of knowledge as experience (ஞான அநுபூதி) and play with the devotees at the feet.

source_issues: Song 1172: the last word is spelt பெறுமாளே for பெருமாளே.
Song 1174: corrupt character in மடலு஡ர்தற்கு (line 398, probably மடலூர்தற்கு, 'to ride the palmyra horse').
Song 1180: the first half has five lines where the pattern needs six; a line seems lost after line 524.
Song 1181: unflagged garble '....... ; ளையோனே' at line 563, probably இளையோனே.
Song 1182: several lines look garbled (பெங்கும் line 573, பூன்கண் line 574, lines 576 to 578).
Song 1185: corrupt character in தசக்஡ண (line 658, probably தசக்ரீவ, Ravana); the ஡ண for ரீ pattern.
Song 1186: unflagged garble யற்முதுடை at line 671.
